utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I apologise. The Chamber was delayed a few minutes this morning. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning. We would call as our next witness, Mr. Ferat Sopi, if that is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sopi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that is offered to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sopi.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where do you presently live, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I was born in Lapusnik village, Gllogovc municipality. After the war, I live in the city of Prizren in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I am 66 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No. I'm a retired person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before you retired, what did you do for a profession?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I worked in the health service. I worked in a pharmacy. Mainly in the health service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long a period of time did you work in the health service?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I worked 43 years, until I retired. From 1961 onwards until now that I retired when I turned 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: First of all, Haradin Bala lives in a village which is not far away from my village. It is called Korretice e Larte, upper Korretice, and we exchange visits. The second, he is a nephew in my village in Lapusnik. Thirdly, he has often come for check-ups in Gllogovc medical centre, and he has received medicine and I have seen him. This is how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that he has come for check-ups in Gllogovc medical centre, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Like all the other patients, he came, because the entire suburbs of Gllogovc know me, and I know them, because that was the only place for them to receive some medical service. There was no other medical centre in that municipality other than the one I worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. My question to you is a bit more specific in dealing with time. Could you tell us when he would come to you for medical treatment. What years did he come to you?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I knew him better in 1991, 1992, and after that, because he was a sick person and came there regularly to get medicine on the basis of a doctor's prescription. With his father, we knew -- we knew each other because his father had a store next to the place I was working, and he was a folk singer, so I knew him. Personally, I didn't have any relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from your treatment of Haradin Bala which you have just told us about in early 1990, did you, as you sit here today, treat or be involved in the treatment of Haradin Bala in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that I knew him from before, and in 1998, in the makeshift infirmary in my home where I, together with some other friends, worked. Like other sick persons he came and received medicine from my personally. I knew him from before, as I said, and whenever he came and he felt the need for taking medicine, he came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you had a makeshift clinic in your home. When did you open the makeshift clinic in your home in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I regret to tell you, sir, that I cannot give you an exact date, but after the events that occurred in our municipality and in particular after the 28th of February, namely the events in Likoshan, Prekaz, and Qirez, the situation became worse, and being unable to go elsewhere to get medicine and for check-ups, I was some ten kilometres away from Gllogovc, so I took some medicaments from the pharmacy and brought them to my house which was situated not far from the asphalt road. So whenever the citizens were in need --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me -- if you could slow down a bit I think it might be helpful for all of us. When you say that you took the medical supplies to your home after the events in February, do you recall whether that was closer to the end of February or the beginning of May when you did this, when you brought the medical supplies to your home to help the people?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: It was by the end of February, after the events in Likoshan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you brought these medical supplies to your home in Lapusnik, did you remain at the same home in Lapusnik during the month of May?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Until the 9th of May I remained in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say until the 9th of May you remained in Lapusnik, could you tell us where your home was in Lapusnik that you remained at until the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had two homes. One was beside the asphalt road, and the other was some 1.200 metres up in the mountain. But I lived in the new house which was beside the asphalt road, Peja-Pristina road. That was where I was situated. But after that, due to the worsening of the situation, I was afraid to remain there because the police and the army used to patrol the road. They fired. They attacked us. So we were afraid. So together with my family, I went to the other house I had up in the mountain. When I left, then I know that on the 9th of May the Serb police forces entered the village. Above my house there is a stone, a rock which is called Glladina. Then they started to fire. We looked at what was happening. At that moment we were eating. The entire family was eating around the sofra, we called it, a kind of wooden table. And we went to the mountains. The police fired at us up the mountains but we were lucky not to get hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you moved to your home away from the asphalt road, what did you do with the medical supplies that you had initially taken to your first home?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: After that -- after that, after the Serb police withdrew from the village, after their forces withdrew, the situation became calmer. And from the house near the asphalt road, I transferred the medical supplies to the other house because I had two spare rooms and they were suitable to hold these supplies, because the population left the village and took to the mountains out of fear, and they were in need of medical supplies because they couldn't go back to Gllogovc. So afterwards, I took the medical supplies to my next house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: About ten days later, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next home where you took the medical supplies, that home, did you work at that home alone or did you work at that home with other people?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No. There were three nurses besides me, but they were young. Some of them -- one of them had just finished school. The others had not. And there was a doctor, a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The doctor who was a general practitioner, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Zeqir Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When did you begin working with Zeqir Gashi at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: After I moved from Lapusnik while we were -- while I was going to the mountain, I hurt my right knee and it got swollen. I had great pains. I went to Berisha. From Berisha I went to a friend of mine with whom I stayed for 12 days. I don't know the exact date. And then I returned. In the meantime, my elder son, together with these nurses and the doctor, transferred the medical supplies I had in the house near the asphalt road to the old house up the mountain. So when I returned home, I found them in those two rooms that I mentioned. And they explained to me that they had brought the medical supplies for me there to administer to the people in need. So Zeqir Gashi -- Ganimete Gashi was the name of the nurse, and two others. Indira Gashi and another. I think her name was Naim. Together with them we stayed until the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll speak to you about the 26th of July in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But before then, what month did that occur in? In 1998, what month did you return and see Dr. Gashi and others working at your home in this makeshift clinic?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: In the month of May, around 20, 25. I cannot give you an exact date, but around that date. From the 20th to the 25th. So the second half of May. But I know that it was the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the month of May when you were at the makeshift clinic with Dr. Gashi, did you see Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I have seen him. I have seen him because he came to the clinic for check-ups and to get medicine. I remember giving him medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you remained at this makeshift clinic until, I believe, July 26, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, apart from treating Haradin Bala at the makeshift clinic, did you have occasion to treat any other of the gentlemen who are sitting in this room at that clinic?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to tell you that the makeshift clinic was available to all the citizens in need who got sick while they were staying in the mountains. Whoever came there, we provided assistance. Not only to Haradin but to everyone who needed it, both soldiers and civilians. Irrespective of what nationality they belonged to, we provide assistance, as much as we were capable of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I know -- I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion before you left the makeshift clinic in July of 1998 when you treated Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Before we opened this makeshift clinic, you said so? Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. Before July 26, 1998, when you left, did you treat Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: After we opened the clinic, Fatmir was there two or three times, because there is like a crossroads there where people move to and fro. So I have seen him, and he came there to get something for his headache, but he didn't have any serious illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever administer an IV to him or have anybody else or be present while an IV was being administered to him around July 25th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just notice that we're starting lead here. I think that could have been asked in a much different way, just what treatment was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, and I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the fall of Lapusnik gorge -- excuse me. I have to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I have to ask you a question, sir. Before the fall of Lapusnik gorge, right before, did you or did you not have occasion to treat Fatmir Limaj on or about the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: It was precisely on the 25th of July, in the afternoon hours, Fatmir Limaj came in a very sick situation. And when he entered the room, he fell down. He lost his conscious. He was unaware. His eyes were closed. We took him from the door. We dragged him to a better place, and we administered him an IV drip as the doctor prescribed. We wrapped his eyes with an ointment because they were red and swollen. I don't know whether he was in a position to see who we were, but we saw him very well. He was moving his hands even though when you get an IV drip you shouldn't move your arm. So I personally kept his arm. So this happened on Saturday, on the 25th, when the fighting in Lapusnik occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you treated Haradin Bala in the month of May. As you sit here today, do you recall whether or not you treated Haradin Bala in the months of June or July?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I regret to tell you, but I really don't know because we moved a lot. I know that in the beginning of May I treated him, but later on I really didn't pay attention because there were others who came for treatment from the civilian population and the soldiers as well. So to tell you the truth, I don't know whether I saw him after the month of May. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, have you had an opportunity to follow these proceedings either by television, radio, or newspaper?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity. We have followed it, but partially because sometimes there's no electricity, sometimes there is. But most of it, yes, we have followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to have a conversation with members of the Prosecution concerning your following these proceedings on television? Did you meet at any time with members of the Prosecution, maybe about a month ago, and talk to them about this case?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd rather we don't -- I don't think that's relevant

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. And a translator who spoke your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. language. If you want, we can move to redact that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: About how long a period of time did you spend talk with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: According to our tradition, I received them as guests. I didn't know why they came to see me. I didn't want them to interview me, and I didn't want to give them an interview regarding these events. I did invite them in because, as I said, our tradition is to receive guests because they found me on the way to my house. I was playing chess in a tea shop, so I invited them in. I offered them coffee or tea, and they told us that -- they told me that they had something official with me, and I told them that I wasn't ready -- for anything official, that I have completed that era in my life of giving statements and interviews. So this was what happened. My attitude was not to give them any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you've said. My question was: About how long did you take with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Well, how long does it take to have a coffee or tea? Ten or 15 minutes. I don't think they stayed longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you met with them were you asked any questions about watching television concerning these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, they asked me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you asked any questions about reading the newspaper concerning these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They asked me this question. But I think now and even then that that was like a free conversation, nothing official, something to talk about while someone is having coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were speaking with them was anybody that you know taking notes?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: One of them, I don't know who it was, a laptop, something like this, he opened it. He tried to write, and then I told him, "Please don't write anything. Put it back because I am not ready to give any statement." We call it a statement. And he didn't write. He didn't even take notes. I told him not to do that, and he didn't. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did anybody at that time have a tape recorder or show you a tape recorder? They were tape recording your conversation with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I didn't see it. Whether he had, I don't know, but personally I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the conversation that you had with them, did you -- did you tell them that you had read the newspaper concerning Dr. Zeqir Gashi's testimony?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me. He asked me whether I saw his testimony on TV, and I said yes, partially, and he asked me why not all of it. I said because there was no electricity all the time. And he asked me then if I read about it in the newspaper, and I said yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you discussed reading about it in the newspaper, did he ask for your opinion or what you thought regarding whether or not everything that Dr. Gashi said being accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's extremely leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, but I beg to differ, and rather than to fight the issue, Your Honour, I'm happy to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will save time and will end in the same result, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you tell the people that you met with that day, Mr. Whiting and any others, what you thought of Dr. Gashi's testimony?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: He asked me, "Did you read it?" I said, "Yes, I did." And he said to me, "Was it the way he described it?" And I said, "Well, there were three pages of interview. Somewhere it is how it was, somewhere it's not. Now, I cannot go into details for each and every question. Some parts are true and some are not."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with him or with the members of the Prosecution about whether or not you would be willing or unwilling to have a formal interview with them if members of the Defence were also present?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question again. Did you have a discussion with them in which you said that you'd meet with them for a formal interview if members of the Defence were present?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I would have accepted to give an interview not only to them but to any other party if I had someone who would advise me. This was unexpected for me. I was outside in the town. They came and fetched me and told me that, "We are here about this issue," so I wasn't ready to give any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you presently are living, I believe, in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your home where you had the makeshift clinic, is that a home where you could presently live?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: This is a question that I asked these gentlemen who came to see me, because they said they saw my house where I used to live. But this, as I said, was just a friendly conversation. I didn't know that an interview was going to be brought up. And then I asked them, "Did you see the house was levelled to the ground?" They said, "Yes." And I asked the interpreter to translate it properly, that I had built that house for my old age, as a place where I could retire. It's in a very good area, mountainous area where the air is very clean. And I asked them, "What did I do to them, to Serbia, for them to level my house to the ground? I had the pharmacy there to help the citizens. Did you see what they did to my house? Why don't you charge them for what they do, not only to me but to the entire village?" And then they saw where I was living, in a small room in a small house where they came to see me. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sopi. Please remain there. There may be others to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No questions thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the first time in this trial I'm going to ask for a little time before I decide whether I have any questions for this witness. I know it's very early in the session, but I wonder whether I could have ten minutes or maybe Your Honours would want to take the first break a little early.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would join in that request, Your Honour, because the 65 ter in this case is seven sentences. It doesn't mention Haradin, Bala, it doesn't mention Fatmir Limaj, and I wouldn't mind a few moments to talk before we begin the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume - excuse me - at five minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I thank Your Honours for the early break which has been productive in this sense that Your Honours are not going to hear any questions from me. I've had a very helpful brief conversation with Mr. Nicholls and he understands my position, and all being well, there will be no necessity for me to ask this witness anything, and I certainly don't ask him anything at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sopi, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have just a few questions for you today. If you don't understand me at any point, let me know right away, okay?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're living in Prizren now, but you spent most of your life in Lapusnik, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we know that you still have a large extended family living in Lapusnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Correct. I have two sons living there. They are married. Each of them has four children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I want to ask you about is just where some places are in Lapusnik, so I'm going to show you an aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a new one, Your Honours. It's an image 9 of P001. However, it has some new markings on it. And it's also in Sanction if anybody wants to look there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll wait for you to put your glasses on. Yes. We have it on the ELMO so that you can point if necessary. Now, the first area I want to draw your attention to, sir, is the red square marked D on the map. That's towards the middle, towards the bottom of the image. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I see number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not number 2. D is what I'm referring to is marked.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can see letter D, yes. It's a red square. And I see number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Within that red square is the clinic that was in the Sopi compound; correct? I know you may not have looked at aerial images before, but can you tell that that's true?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I am not able to understand properly this square, but in my house there was a clinic. This is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not the question. In that red square, if you can tell, just look at the image for a moment, that's your house that -- in Lapusnik which was not close to the Pristina-Peja road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a difficulty here which is the manner in which Mr. Nicholls is asking the question. If the witness can identify the area, that's fine, and work with an aerial map, that's good, and I'm sure that that way Mr. Nicholls can achieve the answers that he wants. However, if the witness is having some difficulty, then he needs to spend some time with the map to try to orient the witness to it as opposed to assuming facts that this witness may not be able to testify to. I think it's really a question of recognition and he's moving a bit quickly, and I'd like this to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm happy to let the witness spend as much time as he needs to look at it. It's cross-examination. I think I can direct him to areas on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No question of that, Mr. Nicholls, but aerial maps are many things that people are not used to and some people cannot adjust to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me give you a couple of other reference points and see if that helps you, sir. There's a big red circle to the left of square D, and in it are three squares marked A, B, and C. Do you see that section? Yes, you're pointing to it.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You see the square --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the area in the square which is marked with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I suggest to you that that is a compound owned by Gzim Gashi. Do you think that's right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I know very well the house and the yard of Gzim Gashi's house because we are neighbours. But in the map it's difficult for me to identify things. I may make some mistakes, and for that I apologise beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: If this is the house of Gzim Gashi, I know that it is Gzim Gashi's house because I know that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And between the Ferat Sopi house marked in D and Gzim Gashi's house in B, does that familiar to you, the field which is in between them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell that now. Yes. It's this field here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've looked at it for a while. I'll just ask you one more time. If you can't tell, that's fine. If you can be sure, that's fine. Is the area in the square marked D the location of your house in Lapusnik where the clinic was? If you can't tell from looking at this map, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Maybe it's the same place. I really am not clear, and I'm sorry, but in the map I can't be sure, because I see some small marks. I know my house, of course, or the location of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll leave that, then, if you're having difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this into evidence. He's had some difficulty with it, but for the record it will be clear what he was looking at and what these questions pertain to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the record may be much ahead of me, but it's not clear to me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it may not be, but he's looked at the area in D, said he wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Looked at B said that may be Gzim Gashi's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that going to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I think it may, Your Honours, because it -- I accept he's had difficulty with the map, but it will show what his questions and answers -- which areas he was talking about and was directed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These locations have been talked about by other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, they have been, but this purports to identify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certain things that have been talked about by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But no witness has satisfactorily identified the markings as the places they've talked about. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We won't receive the aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you some photos now. This may be easier for you. The first one is U0083697. If that could be put on the ELMO. The ERN numbers are very difficult to read on these photos. The one I'm referring to is the photo of a wall with a gate. So that's, I believe, not the correct one that's on the ELMO now. That's right. Sir, could you take a moment to look at that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can see, and I know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that one of the entrances to your -- to the Ferat Sopi -- to your compound in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: This photo shows the entrance of my -- of the upper -- of the lower side of my house. This is on the lower side. It's my -- I put it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have U0083690. Those numbers are on the top right hand of the photographs in small letters. I can assist the usher if necessary. It's a photograph of a building being seen through the trees. That's right. Sir, take a moment to look at that photograph.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at it, but I don't remember what it is. I can't identify anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you see the white building through the trees which is directly above where your pointer is at the moment? That building, yes.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: This one? This one here? Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll suggest to you that that is Gzim Gashi's compound seen from the house you just described in the last photo we looked at. Can you recognise that or are you unable to?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Give me a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take all the time you need. This would be the view down the field we talked about towards Gzim Gashi's compound.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: In this picture I am not sure, because Gzim Gashi's house has two storeys and is taller, and the house I look at now seems to be of a lower height. This one could be just a room, an oda. Gzim's house was near this oda but it was taller. That's why I'm confused, because I see they are in the same height.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question and see if it helps you. Do you see on the bottom portion of that photograph just to the left of where your fingers are there's a part of a brick wall. Do you see that? Down lower. Right on the very bottom of the photograph against the white border. It's where your fingers are on the photograph right now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Here or here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Below, down. Right against the white border on the bottom towards the left of the photograph. Exactly. I suggest to you that's a corner of the wall of your house. Does that help you looking at this photograph? That's one of the corners of the wall surrounding your house. Can you tell that that's Gzim Gashi's compound down the hill?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: This cannot be the wall of my house. Maybe it is, but it seems to be a -- far, far away from here. I think my house stands above Gzim's house. Maybe it is, but I can't see even the wall properly. I just see a red sign here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Nicholls, I believe that was actually the photo ending 3696 rather than 3690.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe you're correct, Your Honour. I'm sorry. As I said, I have a lot of difficulty reading red on green. It's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if it is helpful to you, the photograph ending 3690 may show the house in a perspective nearer to that which the witness is accustomed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've jumped right to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And 3693 might show a little more of the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may. Could we have 3690, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a moment to look at that photo, sir. Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. I see it. The white one here and this wall here, from that I can see that it must have been Gzim Gashi's house. But I am confused because the other house was not there then. He must have added it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: And this wall is the wall of his yard. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you're clear that the white house you pointed to, which is the large white house in the foreground of the photo with a pole in front of it with a sign is Gzim Gashi's house?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. I know. I can recognise it. This must be it. Yes. There is a pasture above his house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Lastly, U008 -- it's actually 3695, I believe. Take your time, sir. Look at that.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just if you can, are you familiar with this view? Can you tell this is a view from the area of your house down to Gzim Gashi's compound through the -- seen through the trees?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: It must be this one, this white one here. This must be the house of Gzim Gashi. I think so, because the picture is not very clear. But I'm looking at other signs, because I know that there wasn't any other house. The other houses were lower, so I think it must be Gzim Gashi's house, even though it is very unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we give the witness a black pen to circle Gzim Gashi's house on this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I'm trying to figure it out properly, because Gzim's house has a road or a path passing by, and I can't see it. From the area I'm looking at, it seems like this one that is Gzim's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you circle it, please.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I circled it. I hope it's this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this would be the view looking down from your house, down the hill?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: This should be it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd move to exhibit the three which he has positively identified, 3690, 369 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you went back to 3696, having seen 3690, you may have more luck, Mr. Nicholls, if you see any point in it. Otherwise, we'll receive the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll take a chance, then, Your Honours. If we could have 3696 back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's easy to be led astray by a judge, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have 3696 again, please. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, one more time. Please take your time to look at that. Tell me if you can see Gzim Gashi's house in this photo now that you've looked at some other photos.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you circle that, please, as you did on the other photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness could be given the pen again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I just want to clarify something in order to avoid misunderstandings. Gzim Gashi's house is taller than all other houses, and from this angle it looks like it's not that tall. It looks as if it's on the same height with other houses. I must be wrong, but as I see it from this angle, it is of the same height with the house that you asked me to circle. This house here, the one-storey house, looks like the room, but it's of the same height, the two-storey one from this angle with the one that is the one-storey one. Maybe I am wrong, but it is confusing me a little bit because from this angle it looks like it is a one-storey house. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is no need for you to apologise. I'll suggest to you that you're looking at Gzim Gashi's house down the hill, and what you're able to see is the top floor. If you can recognise the house, please circle it; and if you're not sure, you don't need to.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I know Gzim Gashi's house, but specifically on this picture I have my suspicions because as you can see, this house here is on the same level with the one-storey house. Now, if I circle it maybe it's wrong. If I don't circle it, maybe again it's wrong. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, don't circle it. We're done with that photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll receive three, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry to have delayed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's all right, Your Honour. Your Honour, I think it's -- that's correct. It should be 3690, 95 and 97 as one exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P251, the three photographs, the three images.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, you first met with the Defence for Haradin Bala in Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that in Prizren or Lapusnik or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: In Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just once. And you spoke with them for quite some time in order to make a written statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just one second, please. I, on that day, as I said, was playing chess downtown. My brother came. He was very angry. He said, "Get up and come home. Some people from The Hague are looking for you." So I just stood up, left the game unfinished, went to my house, and in the road in front of my house I met them, greeted ourselves. So they told me, "We're here to take a statement." And I said to them, "Welcome to our Kosova." And they said to me, "Let us sit somewhere and talk." And I said, "No. You will come to my house. We will have a coffee or tea. And as for statements, there's nothing we can talk about."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: So I went inside their car and then we went to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm talking about when you met Mr. Bala's attorneys, probably Mr. Guy-Smith. Have you met Mr. Guy-Smith in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you met Mr. Harvey in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who did you meet for Mr. Bala's Defence team in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Let me think of his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may be from one of the other occasions.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I know his name. He's from Korretice. Yes, I met him, and they told me to give a statement. I gave a statement. His name was Zeqir Bekolli, yes. He told me to give a statement for Haradin Bala. I gave him my statement. I signed it. I don't know whether he is here now or not, but I gave my statement to him, and whatever I said in that statement, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was about three or four pages typed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. Two pages maximum. It wasn't that long. Two to three pages I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you arrive in The Hague before your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I arrived in The Hague yesterday at 7.30, at the airport, and here around 9.00, 9.30, at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to meet with Mr. Guy-Smith who has kindly stood up for us, or Mr. Harvey, who also stood up, before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Who are they, if I may see them? Oh, these two. Yes. I met them last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You met them last night.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: In the hotel while I was dining.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you go over your statement with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't have any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you talk about your testimony here today with them?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: We discussed briefly, not in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was one of the things you discussed your reading of Dr. Zeqir Gashi's testimony in this case? Is that something you discussed? That's the only question, is whether you discussed it.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: At the hotel, they asked me, "Did you give a statement?" And I said, "No, I didn't give any statement." "How come they said so?" I told them I was not going to give any statement. And they said, "No. You gave a statement, and you spoke of Zeqir Gashi." And I said, "No, that's not true." I told them that I received them in my house, offered them a coffee, and then they said to me, "No, you gave a statement." I said, "No, that's not true. It's possible they have written something without my approval." This is what I told them last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Answer the question, please. Did you discuss with the Defence whether you had read Dr. Zeqir Gashi's testimony in the press?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: He asked me, "Did you read this?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Is it the way you've described?" I said, "Yes, partially."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll get to that. You've answered the question, you discussed it. I'd like to give you a copy of the article, the transcript in Epoka E Re that you read. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm standing to assist my client. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, listen to my question. This is the transcript that you read of Dr. Zeqir Gashi's testimony, isn't it, in Epoka E Re?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember testifying just a few minutes ago -- you don't need to read that. I'm done with that now.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I was just glancing at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. You remember testifying about how you met with Mr. Whiting and Mr. Lehtinen at your house in Prizren. That was on May 4th; right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't remember the date, but correct, I met them in Prizren and they were in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was last month; right? You don't need --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You explained you extended them your hospitality, invited them in and gave them something to drink; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've answered the question. You explained that you were a Defence witness and that you had met with the Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were asked whether you would like to discuss your testimony, and you said you would check with the Defence and get back to Mr. Whiting and Mr. Lehtinen, and they left you their business cards; correct?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In fact, you never called either of those men back. There's nothing wrong with that, but you didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I told them that, yes, and they left me their phone numbers, and I intended to contact them and discuss it with them, but my wife is very ill, so some things came up and that's why I couldn't contact them. She suffers from high blood pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: That's why I couldn't contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were asked one question. You were asked whether you had seen Dr. Gashi's testimony. You answered that you had seen it except for some power cuts, and then you offered that, however, you had read the transcript of the testimony in the newspaper and you thought that everything Dr. Gashi said was accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: What you're saying is correct. What I said there was that I had seen Zeqir Gashi's statement, partially, I have read it in the newspaper, but I had not analysed it in details because, as you can see, it's very long. There were things that were true, and there were things that were not true, and this is what I told them that day and this is what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I'll put it to you that's not what you told them that day. You read the transcript because of the power cuts, and you said that it was all accurate. I'll give you one more chance. That's what you said when you met Mr. Whiting and Mr. Lehtinen in May; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't believe that it's appropriate to talk about giving anybody chances or not giving people chances, one more or any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told Mr. Lehtinen and Mr. Whiting that you'd read the transcript in the newspaper, the one which I've placed before you, and that everything Dr. Gashi said was accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No. I really apologise here, but let us be clear on this. The -- sir, I don't know who they were, these two who came to my house. He asked me, "Did you see his entire testimony?" I said, "No. I just partially followed it because there was no electricity." Then he asked me whether I read about it in the newspaper. I said, "Yes. I read it in the newspaper." And, "Was it true?" I said, "Yes." But as I said earlier, I will repeat it now, partially it is correct and there are things that are not correct. We didn't analyse it in details. Some things skipped to me. I didn't read it entirely. This is what I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it, sir, but that's not what you told them, and you know that. You've changed your testimony since coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I've had occasion in the past to put to you that you do not ask questions, you make assertions and then move on. And you've done it then again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like him to have a chance to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Put it then, "Did you say this," not say "You said it and now I'll move on."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was meant as a question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it comes across differently and it can confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All you were told by Mr. Lehtinen and Mr. Whiting was that the transcript you had read was accurate; right? That's a question, sir.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: I have repeated my answer three times now. I told him that it is partially correct, not entirely correct. I did not analyse it in details to see whether every word in it is correct. It is true that I had told them that partially it was correct and that not everything what he said was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move the Epoka E Re article into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Before that's done, could I mention the last exhibit I believe is P251, not P351 as appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the article will be given Prosecution Exhibit number P252.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. I missed the number of the last exhibit. 252. Could you please give Mr. Sopi a copy of 252.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to you take a look at the exhibit just introduced by the Prosecution. The very first column of this exhibit, this article. And if you look at the very first column under where there's a name it says Burim Etemaj, Bajram Lani, I believe. I may have pronounced them incorrectly. Do you see where those names are in the very first column? At the top. The very top, sir. Do you have that? Mr. Sopi? At the beginning where the names of the journalists are. Do you see that? Mr. Sopi?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: No, I haven't found those names that you just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Do you see in the very first column of the paper, sir, the word Pristina? At the very top. 11 Prill, which I assume is April?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. If you would -- from there --

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you would count down with me one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight lines. On the eight lines do you see it starts with a word that looks like "Prokurorise." I may be pronouncing that incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you -- could you read the next part of the article starting with the words "Zeqir Gashi" to the end of that paragraph. Could you read that out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: "The witness: Answer: My name is Zeqir Gashi. Prosecution: Do you understand me? Witness: Yes. Very well."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before that it, sir, it says: Zeqir Gashi "i cili giate," I think. I'm not doing this well in terms of pronouncing your language. But do you see where it says that?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "Peter Norbert Bouckaert testified that the Prosecution witness, Zeqir Gashi, who during May, June, and July of 1998 worked as a doctor at a clinic in Lapusnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you read that, that was accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you to go over to the next column of the newspaper. And I would like you to go down -- at the next column there is -- it starts and it's in bold letters, it says "deshmitari."

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: In the beginning, on the top of the column?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the top of the column. It says "deshmitari" and it says "prokurori." Then "deshmitari" again; "prokurori" again; "deshmitari" again; "prokurori" again.

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then there is the next line it says "prokurori." And what does it say right there?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What is the question that the Prosecutor asked Dr. Gashi according to this article?

utterances.speaker: FERAT SOPI
utterances.text: "Prosecutor: In May 1998, were you working at your clinic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you read that, that to your mind was accurate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we're still on redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your objection is well-founded, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should just say because of the time we had portions of this translated which can be submitted, but we will submit as soon as possible a full translation of the Epoka E Re article if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because I said I had no further questions, I would appreciate it if Mr. Sopi could be relieved so that he can quickly get to the airport and get back on a plane since he was allowed to come for a very brief period of time here. At this point, I would extend my thanks, and I think all of our thanks to the Canadian government for expediting his quick travel here and the ability to return back to Canada to visit his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Sopi, thank you very much. The questions that are sought to be answered by you have now been completed, and we -- you may now leave and return to your family, it seems, in Canada. So thank you. The court officer will show you out, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all very much, and I wish you a pleasant work, and for these accused to be released as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have one remaining viva voce witness for today's proceedings, and he will be questioned by Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we start with Mr. Puka, I just wonder whether you would like to give an indication of when you would like to take our next break, given that we've had a rather chopped-around morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will run to the normal tape time. About 25 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that fits in with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sure it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puka. Would you please read allowed the words that are on the card given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puka.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a number of questions and then there may be other gentlemen who have some questions for you. If there is anything that I ask you or that they ask you that you don't understand or you'd like clarification, please stop me or them and ask us to make our questions clearer. Okay?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is it correct you were born in 1959? That would make you 46 years of age, I believe, now.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And do you live in the village of Javor.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Have you lived there all your life?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what is your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I'm a farmer. I work in my land.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Have you ever met Mr. Haradin Bala who sits in the middle behind me?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, during the war. From June until the end of August. By the end of June until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how you came to meet him?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. The first time I saw him was when Commander Kumanovo brought him to my house during an evening in late June. I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember now how you're able to say that it was late June rather than early June or July?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: The reason I remember it is because in the first week of July, we began to mow the lawns, and that's why I remember that it is in this period, in late June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The translation we have is lawns. I'm not sure if that's the agriculturally correct expression. What were you cutting, sir?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. We mowed the grass that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're mowing the grass for what purpose? What did you do with the grass? Forgive me. I'm a city boy.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: We feed our animals with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This is hay for feeding the animals?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, hay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you start cutting that in early July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: That's correct. In the first week of July we begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At the time that Haradin Bala first came to your house it was before you had started cutting the grass?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And is there any reason why you wouldn't cut the grass later than the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: The reason is that the grass is ripe at that time. If you leave it for a longer period it will be rotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And no good for feeding the horses or the cows.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When Kumanova and Haradin Bala came to your house, what did he do? Did he stay in your house or did he leave?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And whereabouts in your house did he stay?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: In a room, in an oda. In the guest room --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your oda.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: -- we have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was it just Haradin or did others stay in that oda?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: For the first time it was only Haradin who stayed, then some soldiers came. I don't remember exactly when. Maybe after two or three days. But that night it was only Haradin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And for how long did he remain staying with you in your oda?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He stayed from June until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What happened at the end of August that makes you remember that period?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: After the fall of Luzhnice, we all left that place. After that I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, is your oda separate from the house in which you sleep?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What kind of distance separates them?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: It is about 30 metres far from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so in order for Haradin Bala and the other soldiers to go in and out of the oda they don't have to pass through your house?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, they don't. Because it is -- there is a separate entrance. It has an entrance from the yard, but there is another entrance from the other side where there is a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. So during this period from the end of June until the fall of Luzhnice, did you see Haradin Bala every day or most days or once or twice? How often?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I saw him often, but I can't tell you that I saw him every day because I didn't have to, but I recall that I saw him quite often. I had to tend to my own businesses which I had to do then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Of course. Did you have conversations was him during that period?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. We sat together. We talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did you observe his -- his physical condition at all, what his health appeared to be like to you?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: At that time, he seemed very weak. He seemed to have an ill health. He could hardly stand on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you observe him leaving your village to go anywhere else at any time?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He told me sometimes that he was going either to visit his family or to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you know where he went to visit his family?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you know where he went to visit the doctor?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I am not clear about the question. I am not clear about your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When he told you he was going to see the doctor, did he tell you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. He often told me he was going to Shale, Sedlare, or Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You understood that he was a soldier in the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At that time were you yourself a soldier in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was there any reason why you were not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't have any reasons, but I think an entire people cannot join a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Somebody has to do the farming; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you know what he was doing as a soldier at that time and where he was doing it?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He told me that he was responsible for logistical issues in Luzhnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And how far is Luzhnice from Javor?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Luzhnice may be about two or two and a half kilometres away from Javor. At least from the place where my house is, because it may be even closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you yourself go to Luzhnice during that period? That's the period of end of June until the fall of Luzhnice at the end of August.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Only once I went to Luzhnice, but I remember I was there before Haradin Bala came, when Kumanova was with some three or four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So did you ever see Haradin Bala in Luzhnice yourself?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you've mentioned that he sometimes appeared too weak to walk. How did he get -- if you know, how did he get from your house in Javor to either Luzhnice or Shale or the other places you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: When I saw him, he was driving a white Lada. In a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Puka. If you would remain there, please. There may be some other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puka.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My name an Alex Whiting. I'm one of the Prosecutors with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You recall we have in fact met before at your house in Javor at the beginning of May 1998 [sic]. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. On the 6th of May, and we had a coffee together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right. And I was with an investigator, Mr. Lehtinen, and an interpreter. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the house we met at in Javor is the house that you've been testifying about; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's fair to say that that house is a little bit isolated in Javor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: It's a little bit isolated, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at the end of quite a long road and there aren't really any houses around you, are there?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, to drive to Luzhnice it's more like three kilometres, isn't it, if you drive there on the road, because the road doesn't go directly to Luzhnice, it goes kind of around and would you say it's about three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. In the past, but now the road is damaged, and maybe two and a half or maybe even three kilometres. I never measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for rising but there is a rather obvious error in the transcript. At page 41, line 10, Mr. Whiting is reported as having suggested that he was in the house in Javor at the beginning of May 1998, which even by the efficiency of the Prosecution's standards here is a little early.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. It was May of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We met in May of this year. Isn't that correct, Mr. Puka?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: We met this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puka, the first time that you ever told anybody about Haradin Bala being at your house at any time was in October of 2004 when you were interviewed by the Defence. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know --

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: In October 2004, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. That's the first time that you told your account; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did you know Haradin Bala's name in 1998 or is that something you found out only later?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: After some time of staying there, he told me that his name was Haradin Bala, but until then we knew him by pseudonym Shala. But even after he told me his real name, I called him Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware of his arrest by this Tribunal in February of 2003?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because I saw it on television when he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you saw that he was being charged with committing crimes in Lapusnik during the summer of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. We heard these charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about the other soldiers you say were staying in your oda. Some of those other soldiers were Gani Shala?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Nexhmi?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, Nexhmi Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Besim Zhurda.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were there other soldiers staying in your oda?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. There were others who came and went, but I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many others came and went during July and August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Maybe six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any of their names?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers that you did remember, Gani Shala, Nexhmi Shala, and Besim Zhurda, those soldiers were staying -- were in your oda at the same time as Haradin Bala; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. I don't remember whether they stayed together at the same time. Maybe the soldiers had other duties and Haradin had other duties, so this I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is approximately the same time. That these soldiers were in your oda in -- during the summer of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. By the end of June until August. On the 25th of August. After that, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that during July -- well, let me ask you this before I ask you that question: Were these soldiers staying -- that you've identified staying regularly in your oda from the end of June until August?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember them staying there regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you remember how often they stayed or what they were doing? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember what they did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's hard to remember everything that happened that long ago, isn't it, Mr. Puka.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: It may be hard, but I'll try to tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that Gani Shala was a soldier assigned to Kroimire during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Nexhmi Shala's from Klecke; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And wasn't he in Klecka during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I have seen him several times in my home in the evening or in the morning. And as to where he was staying, this I don't know. But since I have seen him often either in the morning or at night, I thought that he was staying there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you're not sure. Is that right, you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
