utterances.text: I thought that they -- I know that they slept there, but I thought -- I am sure they slept in my house, because I've seen them often there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in fact, Mr. Puka, these men we've been talking about, Gani Shala, Nexhmi Shala, Besim Zhurda, and Haradin Bala all stayed in your house in the fall of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Not in the fall but in the summer, June to August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the summer right now. Do you recall Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that -- let's start with Gani Shala. Do you recall that Gani Shala came to your house sometime maybe in October, maybe November of 1998, and stayed in your house then?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: This happened later. It is true that he came to my house later, but he was also during the time I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's focus on later. Later, Gani Shala stayed at your house and Nexhmi Shala was also there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: What period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We're focusing on the later period, in the fall, maybe October, maybe November of 1998. You've already told us that Gani Shala was there at that time. My question now is that Nexhmi Shala was also there at the same time; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Besim Zhurda was there also?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't remember Besim Zhurda being there?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Haradin Bala was also there; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. From the end of August I didn't see Haradin Bala. I saw him only when he came here to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You never saw him in your house during the fall or late period of 1998. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I'm sorry, I've been told time on the tape is out. We must break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Puka, you're aware that to get from your house in Javor to Shale, Sedlare, you have to drive, if you're driving, to -- first to Luzhnice, then to Klecka and then over to Shale-Sedlare; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you not aware of that or are you suggesting that there's another way to do that drive, to get from Javor to Shale?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. You don't have to go to Luzhnice to go to Shale from Javor. From Javor you can go to Klecke and then to Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you go from Javor to Klecke and then to Shale. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're aware that in June and July of 1998 that was a difficult road to take; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. It was better than it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Really? When did it get better? What was -- let me put that question differently. In -- did you drive on that road in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. No, I did not drive on that road in June of 1998. I didn't have any business to do that. But it was a road that was used by people. I remember I have gone once to get some stones, some limestones that we used to burn for producing limestone, and I know that it was in a better condition than it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that, that you went to get some stones?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: It was before the war. Maybe it was 1997, during the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But during June and July of 1998, you yourself did not drive on that road, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, your memory -- you testified earlier that Haradin Bala stayed in your house until the end of August. That's your memory.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, at the end of June of 1998 or, let's say, from the middle of June until the end of June, you know that there was fighting in Luzhnice; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes, there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 14th of June there was some fighting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the end of June, around the 25th, there was some very intense fighting in Luzhnice?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I heard the sound of fighting. I could hear that even in my house. I could hear the Serb artillery firing, so I could hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the Serb offensive started on the 25th, 26th of July, you know that there were a lot of civilians and soldiers, KLA soldiers and Albanian civilians who had to leave their villages that were attacked; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They had to leave places like Zborce, Carraleve, Fustica, Lapusnik, Malisevo; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't know about those areas because they are far away from where I live. The only thing I know is that we left Javor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you left Javor at the end of August. I'm talking about the end of July. You're aware that at the end of July when the offensive started people had to leave their houses in other villages that were attacked first; right?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. Maybe they had to leave because of the fighting, but I don't know, because at that time I was staying at my home, and I was not interested in asking or in knowing such things, but I know that because of -- probably because of the war the population always leaves the war zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You weren't aware that the offensive had started at that time and that people were moving, there were refugees in the mountains and people were moving from their villages? You weren't -- you didn't hear that at that time, the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that because we are a little bit away from Lapusnik, so I don't know what has happened there. But we know of course that there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when Haradin Bala stayed at your house there would be days that would go by where you wouldn't see him; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He wasn't away for long. As far as I remember, he may have been away for two or three days, but not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us when we came and met with you that it could have been two or three days but in fact you're not sure it could have been longer than that? Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. You asked me whether he was away for a week or so, and I replied that he wasn't away for more than two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after you replied that, do you remember saying but it could have been longer, you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When Haradin Bala and the other soldiers were there, you were busy with your own tasks; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't pay close attention to what the soldiers were doing; correct?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No, I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to put it to you, Mr. Puka, that after six years that you've made a mistake here and that Mr. Bala, in fact, could not have come to your house until after the end of July 1998, not at the end of June 1998. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: It is a fact that he was there from the end of June until the end of August. He was there in my home. He slept there quite often. And I even now remember his Lada car which he used to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Puka, do you accept that it's possible that after so much time has passed that you're making a mistake? Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I may make mistakes. Everybody does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, do you recall telling us when we met with you in your home that sometimes you don't remember what you had for dinner a week ago? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. One cannot remember everything, but some can be remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Puka, you told us that you -- you yourself did not join the KLA. Did you ever suffer any consequences for not joining the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. I didn't join the KLA during that period when the war broke out, but later I did, in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: In Javor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you serve in Javor?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Until the end of the war when NATO troops entered the country. On the 15th or the 16th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say you served in Javor, did you serve in your house or in some other place in Javor?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I asked the question badly. Did you serve in your house in Javor?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: In my house, because there was a unit of the army that was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that unit was stationed in your house from November until the end of the war. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: Yes. From November 1998 until the end of the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever engage in any fighting there?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. During that period, we didn't have any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in the unit?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't remember how many soldiers were in the unit?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: No. Frankly, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Puka, my sympathies. I don't remember what I had to eat last week either. But tell us this if you would, please: When Mr. Bala first came to your house, who was he with?

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: He was with Commander Kumanova. I now call him Commander Kumanova, because at that time we knew him only as Kumanova. But later on we began to call him Commander Kumanova, after he was killed. At that time we knew him only as Kumanova in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you remember.

utterances.speaker: AVDULLA PUKA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when he was killed, whether it was the 23rd of August or 24th or 25th. He was killed in a battle in these three days, in one of them. I was staying with my family. The fighting was going on further from my house. I don't know when I heard about it, but it was on the 25th or the 26th that he was killed in a battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think the Tribunal already has some evidence about that, so I won't trouble you further on it, Mr. Puka. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Puka, thank you very much. That completes the evidence that counsel would like you to give, so you are now free to leave and to return to your home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. As indicated that, that completes the viva voce aspect of Mr. Bala's defence. I indicated the other day that there was a matter with regard to the statement of Mr. Tucker. Just so the Trial Chamber is clear, that is something that is in the process. It will be filed shortly, but it is not yet completed. I had a conversation with Mr. Whiting. We're still working on it to make sure that all Is are dotted and all Ts are crossed and we are in agreement. And once that's completed, we will have that filed with the Chamber, and it certainly will be well within the period of time that has been contemplated in our discussions of yesterday when people were in various stages of wet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And chill.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, and chill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then, subject to the matter of the statement of Mr. Tucker, that closes your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I return to water, cold or warm, please. Your Honours, the Defence bar has discussed in some detail the forthcoming timetable in the light of the position we indicated yesterday with regard to Mr. Musliu. That, of course, still obtains, and the Chamber will recollect there is one outstanding live witness, Professor Wagenaar, to be dealt with, but notwithstanding that, we know that it would be of assistance to both the Chamber and indeed the bar to see if we can achieve either some consensus or some imposition of a consensus as to the timetable to follow. Your Honours, in the discussions we have had, we have very much taken on board what Your Honour said yesterday. Although not written in stone, the very clear thoughts of the Chamber were received loudly and clearly. It is, of course, the custom and indeed the practice at the various bars where we all practice in our home countries for final submissions to follow swiftly if not immediately upon the close of the evidence, even in the longest of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've been known to adjourn at 3.10 to allow overnight, so it's not always inflexibly hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If only Your Honour's generosity was shared by your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. brothers in England. I have been asked to make a speech at the end of an eight-month trial on 4.00 on a Friday afternoon when the evidence finished at 3.00, so I'm sure we all have equal horror stories. But, Your Honour, having said that, the task is a considerable one in the preparation of a document such as the final brief on both sides, and we are not in the business of making life any more difficult for anybody else than it needs to be. But, Your Honour, doing the best we can, and I know this does not find favour across the courtroom, but doing the best we can we have a proposal to put forward tentatively, and it is this: That final briefs be in a position to be, as it were, put on the table, metaphorically speaking, filed, on or about Friday the 8th of July, with a view to what I call final speeches, or submissions if the Chamber prefers the term, to commence the week beginning the 18th of July. Your Honours, that will, given that the Tribunal rises as we understand it for the summer vacation on Friday, the 22nd, given that we know no reason or at least have not been told that the Chamber would not be sitting for the whole of that week, we have contemplated final oral submissions from Mr. Whiting going into two days; Mr. Mansfield a day; Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey - I don't know who it would be - a day; and myself, the final speech on Friday, the 22nd, and I would give the assurance, of course, of being no more than a working day myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say immediately a problem with that. We cannot sit on the 21st and probably the 22nd because of a Plenary. It would be three days of final submission from all counsel, not five, if it was that week. Something that came to my attention last evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But immovable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's immovable for the Plenary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It might mean that oral submissions have to be after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It might mean that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unless they can be accommodated in three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Impossible is the word I hear from my left, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And across.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And across. Yes. I was just about to say. At the risk of making myself even more unpopular by the moment, starting those final submissions the week commencing the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Monday the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm looking at the wrong number. I beg your pardon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's just a weekend after the written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Or the 18th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, anyhow, we will hear what others have to say, Mr. Topolski. We're grateful that you've been able to concentrate thought a little more clearly over the evening as the ice melted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should observe that this proposed timetable is, in terms of presentation of the final brief, not going to be easy, but I'm -- we all understand, from our side at least, possible. A great deal of time is going to be needed to be spent upon it, but therefore what we are saying is both the consensus of our view and realistic. There seems to be no point in seeking to try and curry favour even if we could for one moment by putting forward unachievable dates. But they are, I'm told, achievable. From our side anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything to be added or do you speak for all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, there's nothing to add really except -- I'm just checking dates. I don't know whether bringing forward into the week before, starting on either the 12th or the 13th, would solve some problems. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My turn to be in the cold water. Your Honour, of course the Prosecution will comply with any schedule that it's ordered to comply with. That should go without saying. If we're given these sorts of dates that are being talked about, we will find a way to meet it. I also recognise as the Court said yesterday that finality, efficiency, speed is important. It's not just important to the accused. It's also important to the Prosecution, to the victims in this case, to the interests of justice. However, equally important, in the Prosecution's submission, is getting it right, and that is also important to the accused, to the interests of justice, to the victims, to all the parties, of course, in this courtroom. That goes without saying. The deadlines that we are talking about here are extremely tight. And the Prosecution, it's the view of the Prosecution that while it could meet a deadline of July the 8th somehow, it would provide the Chamber with a better result, a -- one that will be of more use to the Trial Chamber in its deliberations if we were some more time. And I -- I think we would save perhaps some time in the later stages of this process if we were able to do a truly first-rate product, which is what we would like to do. Secondly, I think the rebuttal time that is being talked about is, frankly, very, very tight. Starting -- starting closing -- because we're going to be doing simultaneous filings, of course a big focus of the oral speeches will be to address arguments made by the other side, and time is going to be required to prepare that, and the schedule starting on the 11th or 12th leaves only a matter of days to do that, and I don't think that that will benefit the Trial Chamber. I don't think that will benefit the process if the parties are not given enough time to consider the arguments and submissions of the other side and formulate coherent, clear, well-founded responses to them. Therefore, we would propose that oral submissions be made after the break and that the due date be pushed forward by two weeks to around the 22nd or shortly before, 21st, but sometime during the latter part of that last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, can we pay attention for a moment to what is to come before then, and that is the need to deal with the one additional expert witness, and then there was a suggestion yesterday, I think it was, that there may possibly be rebuttal. Are you in a position at the moment to have assessed whether you will be seeking to lead any rebuttal evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the moment my expectation is that the rebuttal evidence will be very narrow and may not even require calling any live witnesses. It may be that the rebuttal evidence could be accomplished by agreed facts or by one, maybe two 92 bis statements going into evidence. There is the possibility, as we prepare to deal with the expert, there is the possibility -- I think it's very unlikely but I want to be clear about this that there is the possibility that the Prosecution would seek to call an expert in rebuttal. That, of course, would probably throw the whole schedule out of whack, depending on the scope and various agreements we might be able to work out with the Defence. I say the possibility of that is very remote. I cannot make a final judgement about that until we have completed our preparation for this expert. I hope that answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I got the drift clear enough. Now, what view does the Prosecution take on the length of time for final oral submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's very hard to predict, but I certainly would think for the Prosecution a minimum of a day, and it could very well go into a second day. Of course, we will -- having filed our brief we will try to be focused, specific, not repeat things that are in the brief, but we've been told that we're going to be confronted with a 500-page submission from the Defence. Mr. Khan is shaking his head. Maybe because he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the indication given of the completion by the 8th of July may involve some reassessment of that estimate. Can I say given the issues that are alive in the case, it would appear to the Chamber that something very much shorter would do the job, but as we've seen today, Judges can lead people astray.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't -- I certainly don't dispute that. We won't be filing 500 pages. I can assure the Court of that. And I'm sure Mr. Khan will keep it to well under 500 pages for the other side. So it's very hard to estimate for oral submissions, but certainly a day and perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Still with the concerns expressed yesterday afternoon and those of Mr. Whiting today in our ears and conscious that there may be some need for a little flexibility in timetable because of the contingency that could arise because of the expert witness and because what the Defence have very helpfully put forward in response to the Chamber's suggestions made yesterday, because that is in fact not possible because of the Plenary sittings, it seems inevitable, although we had rather hoped it might be avoided, that we cannot complete the process of written and oral submissions before the vacation. That being so, we certainly would think that to give the Prosecution time to deal with the possibility of any rebuttal and/or further expert evidence, we would take the view that fine written briefs should be filed and will give an alternative and hear counsel on it either by the last day before the commencement of the vacation or by the first day of the new term, if you counsel think that the vacation would be of use. Clearly it will not make a practical difference to the Chamber. But we would make it clear that if there is to be any rebuttal expert evidence, it will have to be accommodated before the end of this term, which means that it must be over and done with before the Plenary, which commences on the 21st of July. So if you are led toward some other expert evidence, Mr. Whiting, you'll have to be able to have it available within that time span. In fairness to the accused, we really can't just let this go on beyond that. But for the reasons indicated, certainly extra time in the written briefs should ensure that both sides are in a position to put forward their respective cases in best light and adequately. Now, to enable people after the vacation to have mastered the written brief of the other parties and to be ready with their thoughts, we think the second rather than the first week after the vacation would be appropriate for final oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to interrupt. We certainly don't know the week when the vacation ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're looking at the week of the 22nd to the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any immediate and obvious reason why that is not possible? I see no indication of that. We are a little concerned at the time estimate for final submissions that have been given. What we would propose is that there be one day for the Prosecution and a total of two days for the Defence, and we might be persuaded to allow a half day leeway to each. In other words, in total three or perhaps four days. If there is no other agreement between Defence, we would divide the time equally between each of the three Defence teams. But if there is mutual agreement, of course we would accept that as to some other time division. Just to facilitate people being here, we would, therefore, think commencing Tuesday, the 23rd of August and concluding either Thursday, the 25th or, if necessary, running into Friday, the 26th, but certainly all concluded by that day. I would think at that contains a measure of good and bad news, but I think it is a realistic estimate to ensure in the interests of everybody, including and especially the accused, that we can be sure that the Chamber is provided with well prepared final briefs, that there is an opportunity, if necessary, for any rebuttal evidence to be dealt with, and that counsel are in a position to make final submissions that take account of what has been put against them by the other side and by, in the case of the Defence, by the other accused. Now, that leaves the question whether counsel whether prefer filing final written briefs by the end of term or by the commencement of the next. When I say end of term, it would be, I think, practically the Wednesday, the 20th of July, or it would be the -- Monday, the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, on behalf of the Prosecution, our preference would be the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- we agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "Agreement" is a wonderful word. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is some concern that has been voiced with regard to the dates of argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Contemplating as the Chamber's just proposed the 23rd to the 26th. I understand through quick whispers that it constitutes some difficulties for some of us on this side of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there other dates that are more convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand the week after unless -- the week after would be fine. Any time during the third week -- the third week in August would work. The week beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could just interrupt and ask if the Chamber could rise for a few moments to enable us just between ourselves to discuss these dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us put the options clearly on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First filing of written submissions either by Wednesday, the 20th of July -- I'll make a note of them as I go so I'll remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I'll do so as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or by Monday, the 8th. That is the close of business Monday, the 8th of August. Sorry, I'm one week out already. Monday, the 15th of August, which is the first day of term. And oral submissions either 23rd to, we'll say, 26th August, or if it's going that long we wouldn't need perhaps -- well, it could be the 29th or 30th to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 2nd of September. Those two weeks. Yes. And whether it's a Monday or Tuesday start, again it may be more practical for a Tuesday start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful. I think it would be beneficial if we could just have a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Five. Five, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will take the air. --- Break taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I think we remain agreed with regard to the 20th for filing of the written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We would suggest commencing oral submissions on the 29th, and we would further suggest that we reserve that week for oral submissions. And I think it's fair for me to say that I've been pretty quick. I've tried to keep a narrow and defined focus. My colleagues on this side have also, I think, done the same. I know the extent to which we have worked with the Prosecution in cutting needless examinations and agreeing about things that can be better handled perhaps other ways, and I think it would be fair to say that we probably saved somewhere between five to seven months of just trial time based on all of the things that we were able to agree upon with regard to the experts, which is not insubstantial. There are, in fact, three accused. Our attempts, as you well know, have been in large measure joint, but there are clearly individual concerns for each of these gentlemen which I think need to be addressed fully, fairly, and for all consideration. It's our submission, and I'm sure that my colleagues have something to say with regard to this issue, that to reserve that week would not only be prudent but also equitable and not bring any violence to the -- or violation to the amount of time we have spent in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just add a few observations on the last point. It may seem a relatively minor area, but in one sense it's perhaps the most important area, namely the final oral submissions made on behalf of these three accused. You expressed on behalf of the Tribunal your gratitude only a week or so ago when we closed our case on behalf of Fatmir Limaj in the sense that we had focused on the essential issues which we've tried to do from the very beginning, and I think there can be no question about that on this side, I'm not suggesting on the other side there's been anything different, but on this side there has been a considerable editing and focusing on what is going to be relevant and helpful to the Tribunal, such that I don't know whether it's a trial completed in record time for this Tribunal, but it's certainly a trial completed in one of the shortest times that anyone I've spoken to seems to have known. And therefore, all our estimates, including the estimate I gave for the length of the Defence case -- there's only occasion where I got it wrong in terms of the amount of time for cross-examination. Other than that, our time estimate was three weeks, perhaps four; it was three weeks. And we very carefully indeed considered indeed how much time would be necessary for final oral submissions, addressing material that has not arisen in written form, in other words, responding to the other side, as it were, would take in each case no more than one day, and I think in the context of a case of this gravity with the fact that the defendants themselves are having obviously to wait and they would prefer a sooner schedule, and we have agreed to every single attempt to speed the matter up, including filing and, if possible, final submissions before the summer break. We were prepared to do that. So it's in the context of a great preparedness on our part to complete all deadlines, to focus on the relevant issues, the requests that I would maintain with a certain amount of flexibility, because it may be that Mr. Whiting in the end might just exceed one day. It might be I'll just go under one day. But in the case of Mr. Fatmir Limaj, plainly I have a large number of broader issues to consider as well as the finer detail. So an estimate of one day, I would submit, in relation to a case of this length for that purpose is not excessive and will not be usurping time of the Tribunal in any way at all, so I would ask for reconsideration on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You agree and have nothing to add. Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As ever, the persuasiveness of counsel has its day. We would then see the timetable to be Wednesday, the 20th of July for the filing of written final cases for all parties. Final oral submissions to commence on the Monday, the 29th of August. Prosecution to conclude no later than the end of the 30th and Defence to continue for three days. If Prosecution finishes a day or substantially earlier, we will expect continuous flow. Now, we thank you all for your assistance in seeing that way forward. There will be need, just to make it clear, that we propose now to adjourn until Monday, the 27th of this month, unless it is the Tuesday, the 28th is more convenient. But can I indicate that on the Tuesday it will be necessary, if we have to sit in the afternoon, which is probable, that the Chamber would have to have -- it will be a very short day. The Chamber will probably have to rise about 4.30. So Tuesday, the 28th, if we must sit in the afternoon, of necessity will be a shorter day. And we would sit during that week as is necessary to complete whatever the evidence is that any party needs to offer at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course we can't speak in evidential terms beyond Professor Wagenaar at the moment because there isn't any at the moment. He is available to testify on Monday, the 27th. I think I speak for all when I say we would positively invite the Chamber to hear him on that day. It's going to be very much in Mr. Whiting's hands as to how long he's going to be. My own proposal, because I will be taking him in chief, would be not to be too long with him. So we'll be beholden to Mr. Whiting as to that aspect of the matter. But for a variety of reasons, not least, as it were, getting on with it as best we can, and therefore concluding the evidence if that is going to be the position, we would very much like to call him on the 27th. He's set those days aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Well, we then adjourn now until Monday, the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I just add one rider to that and I don't know whether this is going to be possible or not. I should add the words unless he can be agreed. Over to Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Wishful thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that will be in the afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we have availability during the week if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of June, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
